title: free classes and guru dakshina
hook: should wisdom have a price? a rented room, and no tickets
carry: teaching is a gift; dakshina is the thanks
tomorrow: a week of guests and hosts. which line goes home with you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda walked away from a lecture tour that sold him as a novelty: karma yoga, the work, never its fruits. Today, where he taught instead, and one question.

A good teacher can charge by the minute now: a course, a subscription, a paywall right before the best part. So here's the question: should wisdom have a price? Vivekananda answered with a room in New York. Rented, plain, and crowded. Not enough chairs, so people sat on the floor. No ticket at the door.
screen: `A PAYWALL BEFORE THE BEST PART.` → `SHOULD WISDOM HAVE A PRICE?` → `A ROOM WITH NO TICKETS.`

segments.voice: His disciples' biography describes it simply. In New York he rented rooms and taught classes free of charge: Vedanta, the teaching of the Upanishads, taught as practice, how to sit, how to breathe, how to watch the mind. Out of those classes grew his book Raja Yoga, and his New York work gave the Vedanta Society of New York its start. Why free? Because in Hindu tradition, sacred teaching isn't sold. The old law book of Manu frowns on teaching the Veda for a set fee. Instead the student gives guru dakshina: a thank-you gift to the teacher, offered at the end, from the heart. The Bhagavata tells the most famous one. Krishna and his brother Balarama finish their studies with the sage Sandipani and ask what they can give. The teacher asks for the one thing money can't buy: his son, lost to the sea. Krishna goes all the way to Yama, lord of death, and brings the boy home. That's dakshina: not a price, but a thank-you as big as love can make it. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus sends out his disciples to heal and to preach, and tells them: "freely ye have received, freely give." Shared: what was received as a gift goes out as a gift. An honest difference: in Matthew, the disciples go out on the road and the homes that take them in feed them; in Hindu dakshina, the grateful student brings the gift back to the teacher.
screen: `FREE CLASSES IN A RENTED ROOM.` · `SACRED TEACHING ISN'T SOLD.` · `KRISHNA'S DAKSHINA: A SON RETURNED.` · `MATTHEW: FREELY GIVE.`

segments.voice: If there's paper near you, write down the name of one person who taught you something and never asked anything back. If there isn't, trace the name with a finger on your palm. Then choose a small dakshina for them this week: a note, a call, a dish. Let the gift go back as a gift.
Vivekananda in America: in New York, free classes in a rented room, and the start of the Vedanta Society.
Your line: teaching is a gift; dakshina is the thanks. Rest well tonight.

chat.says: Anaya's mom keeps trying to PAY me for helping Anaya with English. Nani says never take it. why??
options: Nani's thinking like a guru: teaching isn't sold. a fee, no. a thank-you gift, like dakshina, is different.
accepting money would make you a professional, so you'd have to stop.
Nani's just being polite. teaching for free is never very wise.
chat.meaning: In Hindu tradition sacred teaching isn't sold; the student gives guru dakshina, a thank-you from the heart. Nani stretches that to any help given as a gift. Matthew's Gospel says it too: freely ye have received, freely give.

tie.story: Krishna's teacher Sandipani asked no fee; at the end Krishna brought back his lost son as guru dakshina.
tie.friend: Priya can teach Anaya free, and let any thanks come as a gift, not pay.
